public_rationale: A paper public before the post reports language models critiquing their own answers and using their own critiques to improve them. That contradicts the absolute inability under the ordinary functional reading. The evidence concerns trained research systems and bounded tasks. It does not establish formal self-proof, universal reliability or an explicit cognitive world model.
limitations: The result depends on treating independently assessable self-critique as demonstrating an error.
The models received task-specific training and prompts.
Human evaluation of summarization errors was imperfect.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: Current systems do not postulate cognitive models, so they technically cannot prove themselves wrong, because they have no representation of what being right would look like.

statement.excerpt: Current systems simply do not postulate such cognitive models—and so, they technically can’t prove themselves wrong, because they do not even have a representation of what being “right” would look like.
statement.document_title: Three ideas from linguistics that everyone in AI should know

our_interpretation: Current systems means language-model systems existing by June 22, 2022, including fine-tuned systems.
The ordinary functional reading of prove themselves wrong is identifying a substantive error in their own output using relevant facts or task constraints, with the criticism independently checkable.
This does not require a formal mathematical proof or spontaneous correction without prompting.
The claim links the alleged absence of cognitive representations to an absolute inability to establish errors in the system's own answers.
criteria.support_condition: Architecture and controlled evaluations establish both the asserted absence of relevant representations and the resulting inability to identify and substantiate errors in the system's own outputs.
criteria.contradiction_condition: A system available before the post produces independently assessable critiques of its own errors and uses them to improve its answers. That contradicts the claimed absolute inability without proving a particular cognitive architecture.
